# clavis trust

<p class="cli-lead">Trust a server&#39;s self-signed certificate on this computer</p>

<div class="cli-usage">

```sh
clavis trust <command>
```

</div>

Decide which self-signed server certificates this computer accepts.
Certificates from a public authority (Let's Encrypt, your company CA in
the system store) need nothing here.

The first time the CLI meets a self-signed server, it shows the
certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint and asks you to trust it, like SSH does
with a new host. The answer is pinned to the server's public key, so it
survives the yearly certificate renewal and a change of the server's
address. If the key ever changes, the CLI stops with a warning and asks
you to type `trust` to accept the new one.

Compare the fingerprint with the one the server prints
(`docker exec clavis clavis admin tls-info`) or with the one an admin
sent you.

## Examples

<p class="cli-example-title">Trust a LAN server</p>

```sh
clavis trust add https://192.168.1.20
```

<p class="cli-example-title">Trust without a prompt (scripts, onboarding docs)</p>

```sh
clavis trust add https://192.168.1.20 --fingerprint 9E:1C:…:F9
```

```sh
clavis trust ls
```

## Details

Other ways to trust a server, for automation:

- `CLAVIS_SERVER_FINGERPRINT`: the expected SHA-256 of the certificate or its public key. Nothing is saved.
- `CLAVIS_CA_CERT`: a PEM file (or a list of them) with your own CA, added to the system roots.
- `CLAVIS_TRUST_FILE`: where pins are stored, instead of `trusted-servers.json` in the config folder.

To avoid the question entirely, give the server a real certificate: with
a domain you control, set `CLAVIS_ACME_DNS` and the server gets one from
Let's Encrypt even on a private network.
